prompt:
Statements: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants.
Conclusions: I. All roses are plants. II. All plants are roses.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: Since roses are a subset of flowers, and flowers are a subset of plants, roses must be a subset of plants (I follows). Conclusion II reverses the relationship incorrectly: plants can include many things besides roses.

prompt:
Statements: Some doctors are teachers. All teachers are readers.
Conclusions: I. Some doctors are readers. II. All doctors are readers.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: Since some doctors are teachers, and all teachers are readers, those same doctors must be readers, so "some doctors are readers" follows. "All doctors are readers" does not follow, since only some doctors were established to be teachers.

prompt:
Statements: No cats are dogs. All dogs are animals.
Conclusions: I. No cats are animals. II. Some animals are not cats.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: Dogs are animals, and no dogs are cats, so those dog-animals are not cats, meaning "some animals are not cats" follows. "No cats are animals" does not follow, since cats could still be animals of some other kind, just not dogs.

prompt:
Statements: All pens are pencils. Some pencils are erasers.
Conclusions: I. Some pens are erasers. II. Some erasers are pens.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: The pencils that are erasers might be entirely outside the subset of pencils that are pens: the statements don't establish any overlap between pens and erasers. This is a classic syllogism trap where no valid conclusion connects the two end terms.

prompt:
Statements: All squares are rectangles. All rectangles are quadrilaterals. Some rectangles are not colored.
Conclusions: I. All squares are quadrilaterals. II. Some squares are not colored.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: By the transitive chain, squares are a subset of rectangles, which are a subset of quadrilaterals, so all squares are quadrilaterals (I follows). The rectangles that are not colored might be entirely non-square rectangles: no overlap between squares and the "not colored" rectangles is established, so "some squares are not colored" does not follow.

prompt:
Statements: Some artists are musicians. No musicians are engineers.
Conclusions: I. Some artists are not engineers. II. No artists are engineers.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: Some artists are musicians, and no musicians are engineers, so those artist-musicians are not engineers: "some artists are not engineers" follows. "No artists are engineers" is too strong, since other artists (not musicians) could still be engineers.

prompt: Argument: "The city should build a new highway to reduce traffic congestion downtown, since traffic has increased 30% over the past five years." Which of the following is an assumption underlying this argument?
options: Downtown business owners support the project and expect it to bring in more customers.
The city can finance the highway without cutting other transportation projects.
A new highway will not simply attract more cars and eventually recreate congestion.
Reducing traffic congestion downtown matters more than any other problem the city faces.
explanation: The argument assumes the highway will genuinely reduce congestion rather than just redistribute or eventually recreate it through induced demand, a common gap in this type of infrastructure argument.

prompt: Argument: "Since employees who take regular breaks report higher job satisfaction, the company should mandate hourly breaks to improve overall satisfaction." Which assumption does this argument rely on?
options: Employees currently take their breaks at staggered times rather than all at the same hour of the day.
The company has enough staff on hand to cover for everyone who steps away each hour.
Mandating breaks will produce the same effect as employees voluntarily choosing to take them.
How often employees take breaks is the only real influence on their overall job satisfaction.
explanation: The argument assumes a mandated break has the same positive effect as a self-chosen one: the observed correlation between voluntary breaks and satisfaction doesn't guarantee the same result if breaks are imposed.

prompt: Argument: "Reading fiction improves empathy, so schools should require students to read more novels to become more empathetic adults." What does this argument assume?
options: There is no other classroom activity that develops empathy as effectively as reading fiction does.
Students at these schools currently read far fewer novels than students at comparable schools.
Every novel a school might choose to assign builds empathy to roughly the same degree.
The observed link between reading fiction and empathy reflects causation, not just correlation.
explanation: The argument assumes a causal relationship, when the initial claim only establishes a correlation between reading fiction and empathy.

prompt: Argument: "Since the new fitness app has 500,000 downloads, it must be effective at helping people get fit." What is the flawed assumption here?
options: Every one of the 500,000 people who downloaded the app is still using it on a regular weekly basis.
The size of the download count mainly reflects how affordable the app was next to its rivals.
Fitness apps in general produce better physical results for their users than gyms do.
High download numbers indicate effectiveness, rather than just popularity or marketing reach.
explanation: The argument wrongly assumes downloads (popularity) equal actual effectiveness, ignoring that popularity could stem from marketing rather than real results.

prompt: "All members of the hiking club own hiking boots. Sarah does not own hiking boots." What can be validly concluded?
options: Sarah will buy hiking boots soon.
All hiking club members go hiking very often.
Sarah is not a member of the hiking club.
explanation: This is the contrapositive of "all members own boots": if someone doesn't own boots, they're not a member, a valid logical inference.

prompt: "Every time it rains heavily, the river level rises. The river level has not risen today." What can be validly concluded?
options: The river is at its lowest level ever.
It rained only lightly in the city today.
It did not rain heavily today.
It will rain heavily somewhere tomorrow.
explanation: By the contrapositive of the stated rule, no rise in river level means it did not rain heavily today, a valid inference.

prompt: "Sales of umbrellas increase every time it rains in the city. Yesterday, umbrella sales were unusually high." What can be reasonably inferred?
options: The umbrella shop must have lowered its prices sharply yesterday.
It is possible that it rained in the city yesterday.
It definitely rained in the city at some point yesterday.
It will almost certainly rain again tomorrow.
explanation: Concluding it "definitely" rained would be affirming the consequent, a logical fallacy: other factors could also raise sales. Only "possible" is validly supported.

prompt: Five colleagues (H, I, J, K, L) sit in a row of five chairs, numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. J sits exactly two seats to the right of H. I sits immediately to the left of K. L does not sit at either end. K sits at seat 5. Where does H sit?
explanation: K=5, so I (immediately left of K) = 4. The remaining seats {1, 2, 3} go to H, J, L with $J = H+2$. Only H=1, J=3 fits within that set (H=2 would put J=4, already taken). That leaves L=2, which satisfies "not at either end" since seats 1 and 5 are the ends. H sits at seat 1.

prompt: Argument: "The new drug reduces headache duration, since patients who took it recovered faster than those who didn't." Which finding would most strengthen this argument?
options: A few patients in the study reported mild, temporary side effects.
The study group included roughly equal numbers of men and women throughout.
The drug costs more than the headache medications already on the market.
The study was conducted using a randomized, placebo-controlled design.
explanation: A randomized, placebo-controlled design rules out confounding factors, directly strengthening the causal claim that the drug itself caused the faster recovery.

prompt: Argument: "Switching to solar panels will lower the town's electricity costs, based on similar towns that adopted solar and saw savings." Which fact would most strengthen this argument?
options: Solar panel installations have grown steadily across the country over the past decade.
The comparison towns have a similar climate and energy usage pattern to this town.
Electricity prices in the region have risen slightly over the course of this year.
The town has set aside a moderate budget for infrastructure projects this year.
explanation: The argument reasons by analogy: it takes what happened in other towns as evidence for what will happen here. An analogy is only as strong as the resemblance it rests on, so confirming that the comparison towns match this town on the factors that actually drive solar savings, sunlight and how much electricity is used, closes the biggest gap in the reasoning. The popularity of solar panels nationwide says nothing about whether they save this town money, since something can spread widely without being cost-effective. A slight rise in electricity prices describes the status quo the town wants to escape rather than any evidence that solar will beat it. The town's infrastructure budget bears on whether the switch is affordable to make, which is a separate question from whether it lowers running costs.

prompt: Argument: "The new teaching method improves test scores, as shown by a pilot classroom that used it and scored higher than average." What would most strengthen this claim?
options: The pilot classroom had students with similar starting ability levels to the average classroom.
The school introduced new textbooks across several subjects earlier in that same school year.
The pilot classroom held noticeably fewer students than the average classroom in the school.
The teacher who ran the pilot classroom had over a decade of classroom experience.
explanation: Ruling out that the pilot group simply started out stronger strengthens the claim that the teaching method itself caused the improvement.

prompt: Argument: "Company X's new marketing campaign caused its sales to double last quarter." Which finding would most weaken this argument?
options: The marketing campaign relied mainly on social media advertising.
A major competitor went out of business during the same quarter.
The campaign cost noticeably less than the company's previous ones.
Company X has been operating in this market for over ten years.
explanation: An alternative explanation (the competitor's exit) undermines the claim that the campaign alone caused the sales increase.

prompt: Argument: "Since students who attend the tutoring program score higher on exams, the tutoring program must be effective at improving scores." What would most weaken this argument?
options: The tutoring program is offered free of charge to every student enrolled at the school.
Students who choose to attend tutoring tend to already be higher-performing, more motivated students.
The tutoring program has been running continuously for the past three academic years now.
Tutoring sessions are held twice a week in the school library after classes.
explanation: This points to self-selection bias (already high-performing, motivated students opting in) which undermines the causal claim that tutoring itself raised scores.

prompt: Argument: "The new traffic light system must have reduced accidents, since accident reports dropped 15% after it was installed." Which fact would most weaken this conclusion?
options: The city has more traffic lights per resident than any of its neighboring cities.
The city also lowered the speed limit on the same roads at the same time.
The traffic light system was expensive for the city to install and maintain.
Drivers in the area generally dislike the new traffic light system intensely.
explanation: An alternative simultaneous change (the lowered speed limit) offers a competing explanation for the drop in accidents, weakening the attribution to the traffic lights alone.

prompt: A five-story building has floors numbered 1 (bottom) to 5 (top), each occupied by a different tenant: M, N, O, P, Q. O lives exactly two floors above N. P lives immediately below Q. M does not live on floor 1 or floor 5. P does not live on floor 1. Which floor does N live on?
explanation: With $O = N+2$, the only candidate pairs are (N=1,O=3), (N=2,O=4), (N=3,O=5). Testing N=2,O=4 leaves {1,3,5} for M,P,Q, but P and Q must be consecutive floors ($Q = P+1$), and no consecutive pair exists in {1,3,5}, so this case fails. Testing N=3,O=5 leaves {1,2,4}, giving P=1,Q=2,M=4, but this violates "P does not live on floor 1." Only N=1,O=3 works: the remaining floors {2,4,5} give P=4,Q=5 (consecutive), leaving M=2, which satisfies "M is not on floor 1 or 5." N lives on floor 1.

prompt: Seven friends (A, B, C, D, E, F, G) sit evenly spaced around a circular table, all facing outward, away from the table. B sits three seats clockwise from A. C sits immediately to the right of B. D sits immediately to the left of A. E sits two seats clockwise from D. F sits immediately to the right of E. Where does G sit relative to A?
options: Second to the left of A
Second to the right of A
Immediately to the right of A
Third to the right of A
explanation: Numbering seats 1-7 clockwise with A=1: B (three seats clockwise) = 4. C (immediately right of B) = 5. D (immediately left of A) = 7. E (two seats clockwise from D) = $7+2=9$, which wraps to 2. F (immediately right of E) = 3. Every seat except 6 is now taken, so G=6. Going counterclockwise from A (1 to 7 to 6) is two steps, so G sits second to the left of A.

prompt: Seven runners (A, B, C, D, E, F, G) finish a race in distinct positions, 1st through 7th, with no ties. C finishes immediately after A. E finishes exactly three positions after B. F finishes immediately after D. A finishes before B. G does not finish 1st or 7th. In which position does G finish?
explanation: Testing the constraints systematically, the only assignment consistent with all five clues is A=1st, C=2nd, G=3rd, B=4th, D=5th, F=6th, E=7th. This satisfies $C = A+1$, $E = B+3$, $F = D+1$, A before B, and G excluded from 1st and 7th, and no other arrangement of the seven runners satisfies every clue simultaneously. G finishes 3rd.

prompt: Five friends (A, B, C, D, and E) sit in a row of five chairs, numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. B sits immediately to the right of A. C sits immediately to the right of B. D sits at one of the ends. E sits somewhere between D and A. E does not sit at seat 2. What is the order from left to right?
explanation: The block A-B-C occupies three consecutive seats, and D sits at an end. Testing A=1 (so B=2, C=3) forces D=5 (the only remaining end), with E strictly between D and A, i.e. E in {2,3,4}; since 2 and 3 are taken and E cannot be seat 2 anyway, E=4. Testing A=3 (B=4, C=5) instead forces D=1, with E between D and A, i.e. E=2, but that violates "E does not sit at seat 2." Only the first case survives: order A, B, C, E, D.

prompt: Six friends P, Q, R, S, T, U sit evenly spaced around a circular table, facing outward, away from the table. Q sits directly opposite P. R and S occupy the two seats immediately beside Q, with R on Q's right. T sits immediately to the left of S. Where does U sit?
options: Immediately to the right of Q
Immediately to the left of S
Immediately to the left of P
explanation: Number the seats 1 to 6 clockwise and place P at seat 1. Because everyone faces outward, away from the table, each person's right is the clockwise direction. With six evenly spaced seats, the seat directly opposite P is seat 4, so Q sits there. R and S are Q's two neighbours, seats 3 and 5; R is on Q's right, which is clockwise from seat 4, so R is at 5 and S is at 3. T is immediately to the left (counterclockwise) of S, so T is at 2. Seat 6 is the only one left, and it is the counterclockwise neighbour of P, that is, immediately to P's left, so U sits there. Checking the other choices against this arrangement: the seat immediately to Q's right is 5, which belongs to R; the seat immediately to S's left is 2, which belongs to T; and the seat opposite R is also 2, again T.

prompt: Four houses are arranged in a row: House 1, House 2, House 3, House 4 (left to right). The blue house is immediately to the right of the red house. The green house is at one of the ends. The yellow house is not adjacent to the green house. Which house is the red house?
explanation: Testing both possible positions for the green house (House 1 or House 4) and checking the yellow-not-adjacent-to-green constraint, only two arrangements satisfy all conditions: Green-Red-Blue-Yellow (1-2-3-4) or Yellow-Red-Blue-Green (1-2-3-4). In both valid arrangements, the red house is House 2.

prompt: In a certain code, "SUN" is written as "TVO". How is "MOON" written in the same code?
explanation: Each letter is shifted forward by one position in the alphabet (S→T, U→V, N→O). Applying this to MOON: M→N, O→P, O→P, N→O, giving "NPPO".

prompt: In a certain code, each letter is replaced by double its position in the alphabet, so "CAT" (C=3, A=1, T=20) is written as "6-2-40". How is "DOG" written in the same code?
explanation: D is the 4th letter ($4 \times 2 = 8$), O is the 15th letter ($15 \times 2 = 30$), G is the 7th letter ($7 \times 2 = 14$). So DOG becomes "8-30-14".

prompt: If "PAPER" is coded as "QBQFS" (each letter shifted forward by one position), how is "PENCIL" coded in the same pattern?
explanation: Shifting each letter of PENCIL forward by one: P→Q, E→F, N→O, C→D, I→J, L→M, giving "QFODJM".

prompt: Pointing to a boy in a photograph, a woman says, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother." How is the woman related to the boy?
explanation: "My mother" unambiguously refers to the woman's own mother, who has only one daughter. Since the woman herself is female and is a child of her own mother, she must be that only daughter. So "his mother" is the woman herself, making her the boy's mother.

prompt: A is B's brother. C is A's mother. D is C's father. E is D's mother. How is B related to D?
explanation: A and B are siblings, sharing the same mother, C. D is C's father, making D the maternal grandfather of both A and B. So B is D's grandchild.

prompt: Find the next number in the series: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
explanation: Each term follows the pattern $n(n+1)$: $1 \times 2 = 2$, $2 \times 3 = 6$, $3 \times 4 = 12$, $4 \times 5 = 20$, $5 \times 6 = 30$, so the next term is $6 \times 7 = 42$.

prompt: Find the next letter in the series: B, D, G, K, P, ?
explanation: The gaps between letter positions increase by one each time: B(2)→D(4) is +2, D→G(7) is +3, G→K(11) is +4, K→P(16) is +5. The next gap is +6, giving position 22, which is V.

prompt: Find the missing number: 5, 11, 23, 47, ?
explanation: Each term follows the pattern $a_{n+1} = 2a_n + 1$. $5 \times 2 + 1 = 11$, $11 \times 2 + 1 = 23$, $23 \times 2 + 1 = 47$, $47 \times 2 + 1 = 95$.

prompt: A man walks 5 km north, then turns right and walks 3 km, then turns right again and walks 5 km. How far is he from his starting point?
explanation: North 5 km, then right turn (east) 3 km, then right turn again (south) 5 km. The north and south legs cancel out (5 km each, opposite directions), leaving only the 3 km eastward displacement.

prompt: Six boxes (A, B, C, D, E, F) are stacked one on top of another, numbered position 1 (bottom) to 6 (top). B is exactly two positions above A. D is directly above C. E is at the very top. A is below C. F is not at the bottom. Which position does A occupy?
explanation: E=6 (the top). With $B = A+2$ and $D = C+1$, and A below C, testing A=1 gives B=3; the remaining positions {2,4,5} then need C and D consecutive, which only C=4,D=5 satisfies, leaving F=2 (not the bottom, consistent with the clue). No other value of A satisfies every constraint at once. A occupies position 1 (the bottom).

prompt:
Statements: All teachers are educators. All educators are professionals.
Conclusions: I. All teachers are professionals. II. All professionals are teachers.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: By the transitive chain, teachers $\subseteq$ educators $\subseteq$ professionals, so all teachers are professionals (I follows). Conclusion II reverses the relationship incorrectly.

prompt: Eight students are divided into two teams of four for a project: Team X and Team Y. A is on Team X. B is on Team Y. C is on the same team as B. D is on a different team from A. E is on the same team as A. F is on the same team as D. G is on a different team from F. H is on the same team as G. Which team is H on?
explanation: Following the chain: A=X, so E=X (same as A). B=Y, so C=Y (same as B). D is different from A, so D=Y, and F=Y (same as D). G is different from F, so G=X, and H=X (same as G). Team X ends up with A, E, G, H, and Team Y with B, C, D, F, four each. H is on Team X.

prompt:
Statements: Some students are athletes. No athletes are lazy people.
Conclusions: I. Some students are not lazy people. II. No students are lazy people.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: The students who are athletes cannot be lazy people (since no athletes are lazy), so some students are not lazy people (I follows). "No students are lazy people" is too strong, since non-athlete students could still be lazy.

prompt:
Statements: All doctors are graduates. Some graduates are wealthy. No wealthy people are dishonest.
Conclusions: I. Some graduates are doctors. II. No doctors are dishonest.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: "All doctors are graduates" converts validly to "Some graduates are doctors" (I follows). For II, we know the wealthy graduates are not dishonest, but nothing establishes that doctors overlap with that wealthy subset: a doctor could be a non-wealthy graduate who is dishonest, so "no doctors are dishonest" does not follow.

prompt:
Statements: No mathematicians are poets. All poets are dreamers.
Conclusions: I. No mathematicians are dreamers. II. Some dreamers are not mathematicians.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: "No mathematicians are dreamers" is too strong, since mathematicians could be dreamers through some route other than poetry. Since poets are dreamers and no poets are mathematicians, those poet-dreamers are not mathematicians, so some dreamers are not mathematicians (II follows).

prompt: Six colleagues (P, Q, R, S, T, U) sit in a row of six chairs, numbered 1 to 6 from left to right. P sits at seat 1. Q sits two seats to the right of P. R sits immediately to the left of Q. S sits at seat 6. T does not sit at seat 1. T sits immediately to the right of U. Where does U sit?
explanation: P=1, $Q = P+2 = 3$, $R = Q-1 = 2$, S=6. The remaining seats {4, 5} go to T and U with $T = U+1$, so U=4 and T=5 is the only fit (U=5,T=6 is impossible since S already occupies 6). This also satisfies "T does not sit at seat 1." U sits at seat 4.

prompt: Six people (A, B, C, D, E, F) sit evenly spaced around a circular table, all facing outward, away from the table. B sits two seats clockwise from A. C sits immediately to the right of B. D sits immediately to the left of A. F sits immediately to the right of C. Where does E sit relative to A?
options: Third to the right of A
Immediately to the left of A
Immediately to the right of A
explanation: Numbering seats 1-6 clockwise with A=1: B (two seats clockwise) = 3, C (immediately right of B) = 4, D (immediately left of A) = 6, F (immediately right of C) = 5. The only remaining seat is 2, for E, which is the clockwise neighbor of A, i.e., immediately to the right of A.

prompt:
Statements: All library books are catalogued items. No catalogued items are lost. Some catalogued items are reference materials.
Conclusions: I. No library books are lost. II. Some reference materials are library books.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: Since library books are catalogued items, and no catalogued items are lost, no library books are lost (I follows). The catalogued items that are reference materials might be an entirely different subset from the catalogued items that are library books: no overlap between them is established, so "some reference materials are library books" does not follow.

prompt:
Statements: Either the meeting is on Monday or it is on Wednesday. The meeting is not on Monday.
Conclusions: I. The meeting is on Wednesday. II. The meeting could be on Tuesday.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: This is a valid disjunctive syllogism: given the meeting is either Monday or Wednesday, and it isn't Monday, it must be Wednesday (I follows). Conclusion II contradicts the stated either/or, so it does not follow.

prompt: A six-story building has floors numbered 1 (bottom) to 6 (top), each occupied by a different tenant: J, K, L, M, N, O. L is exactly three floors above J. M is exactly one floor above K. N lives on floor 1. O does not live on the top floor. Which floor does J live on?
explanation: N=1. With $L = J+3$ and $M = K+1$, testing J=3 gives L=6; the remaining floors {2,4,5} then need K and M consecutive, which only K=4,M=5 satisfies, leaving O=2 (not the top floor, consistent with the clue). No other value of J satisfies every constraint at once. J lives on floor 3.

prompt:
Statements: No vegetarians eat meat. Some athletes eat meat.
Conclusions: I. Some athletes are not vegetarians. II. No athletes are vegetarians.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: The meat-eating athletes cannot be vegetarians (since vegetarians never eat meat), so some athletes are not vegetarians (I follows). "No athletes are vegetarians" is too strong, since other athletes could still be vegetarian.

prompt:
Statements: All squares are polygons. Some polygons are not colored.
Conclusions: I. Some squares are not colored. II. Some polygons are squares.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: "All squares are polygons" converts validly to "Some polygons are squares" (II follows). But the polygons that aren't colored might exclude every square, so "some squares are not colored" does not follow.

prompt:
Statements: Every scientist in the lab wears a badge. No one wearing a badge is unauthorized.
Conclusions: I. No scientist in the lab is unauthorized. II. All badge wearers are scientists.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: Since scientists wear badges, and no badge wearer is unauthorized, no scientist is unauthorized (I follows). II reverses the relationship: other staff could also wear badges without being scientists.

prompt:
Statements: All melodies are compositions. No compositions are silent. Some silent things are recordings.
Conclusions: I. No melodies are silent. II. Some recordings are not melodies.
Which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
explanation: Since melodies are compositions, and no compositions are silent, no melodies are silent (I follows). Some silent things are recordings, and since no melodies are silent, those silent recordings cannot be melodies, so some recordings are not melodies (II follows).

prompt: Argument: "The company should switch all its delivery trucks to electric vehicles, since electric vehicles have lower fuel costs than gasoline trucks." Which of the following is an assumption underlying this argument?
options: Company drivers would rather operate electric trucks than the gasoline ones they use now.
Electric delivery trucks have already been adopted by most of the company's direct competitors.
The savings from lower fuel costs will not be offset by higher purchase or maintenance costs of electric vehicles.
The price of gasoline will keep climbing over the next several years in this region.
explanation: The argument assumes the fuel savings actually translate into net savings, ignoring the possibility that higher upfront or maintenance costs could offset the benefit.

prompt: Argument: "Because the average reading score in District A is higher than in District B, District A's schools must be providing better reading instruction." What does this argument assume?
options: Reading scores are the only meaningful measure of the quality of a school district's teaching.
District A operates a greater number of schools and therefore reaches more students than District B.
District B employs fewer reading teachers per student than District A currently employs.
The score gap is not primarily explained by differences in students' socioeconomic backgrounds or outside resources.
explanation: The argument assumes the score difference reflects instructional quality rather than confounding factors like students' home environment or economic resources.

prompt: "Every certified technician passed a rigorous exam. Jason did not pass the rigorous exam." What can be validly concluded?
options: All technicians must eventually retake the exam.
Jason will retake the exam next term.
Jason has failed at his job.
Jason is not a certified technician.
explanation: This is the contrapositive of "all certified technicians passed the exam": if someone didn't pass, they aren't certified, a valid inference.

prompt: "In a factory, machines serviced monthly break down less often than machines serviced yearly. Machine 12 broke down frequently this year." What can be reasonably inferred?
options: Machine 12 was definitely serviced yearly rather than monthly.
All machines in the factory will break down eventually.
It is possible that Machine 12 was not serviced monthly.
explanation: Concluding Machine 12 was "definitely" serviced yearly would be affirming the consequent: other causes could also explain frequent breakdowns. Only "possible" is validly supported.

prompt: Argument: "The new packaging reduced shipment damage, since damage complaints fell 40% after the switch." Which fact would most strengthen this argument?
options: Customers were surveyed about the appearance of the new packaging design shortly afterward.
No other change in shipping method, carrier, or handling occurred during the same period.
The company shipped noticeably fewer packages overall this year than it did in the last one.
The new packaging is manufactured entirely from recycled cardboard material.
explanation: Ruling out other simultaneous changes strengthens the claim that the packaging itself (not some other factor) caused the drop in damage complaints.

prompt: Seven students (A, B, C, D, E, F, G) scored differently on a test, ranked 1st (highest) through 7th (lowest), with no ties. C ranked exactly two places below A. E ranked immediately below B. F ranked immediately above D. G ranked 4th. A ranked better than D. B did not rank last. Who ranked 1st?
explanation: G=4th. With $C = A+2$ and $F = D-1$, and A ranked better than D, testing A=3 gives C=5; the remaining ranks {1,2,6,7} then need B and E consecutive with $E = B+1$, which only B=1,E=2 satisfies, leaving D=7,F=6 ($F = D-1$ holds, and B=1 is not last, consistent with the clue). No other value of A satisfies every constraint at once. B ranked 1st.

prompt: Argument: "Employees who work remotely report higher productivity scores, so the company should let all employees work remotely to boost productivity." Which finding would most weaken this argument?
options: The company's lease on its main office building is due to expire at the end of next year.
Employees who currently choose to work remotely tend to be more self-disciplined and have fewer household distractions than the broader workforce.
The company already provides strong collaboration tools for everyone who works remotely.
Remote work saves employees a considerable amount of commuting time each week.
explanation: This points to self-selection bias (the employees who already opt for remote work may be unrepresentative) undermining the claim that remote work itself would boost productivity for everyone.

prompt: Six boxes (P, Q, R, S, T, U) are stacked one on top of another, numbered position 1 (bottom) to 6 (top). Q is exactly two positions above P. R is directly below Q. S is at the very bottom. T is directly above U. T is not at the top. Which position does P occupy?
explanation: S=1, so P, Q, R, T and U fill positions 2 to 6. With $Q = P+2$ and $R = Q-1$, the only values of P that keep Q within the stack are 2, 3 and 4. P=3 gives Q=5 and R=4, leaving positions {2,6} for T and U, but those are not adjacent, so $T = U+1$ is impossible. P=2 gives Q=4 and R=3, leaving {5,6}, which forces U=5 and T=6; that puts T at the top, violating the last clue. P=4 gives Q=6 and R=5, leaving {2,3}, so U=2 and T=3, and T is not at the top, so every clue holds. P occupies position 4.

prompt: Five students (P, Q, R, S, T) sit in a row of five chairs, numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. Q sits at seat 3. P sits immediately to the left of Q. S sits immediately to the right of Q. T sits immediately to the left of P. R sits at the rightmost end. What is the order from left to right?
explanation: Q=3, so P (immediately left of Q) = seat 2, and S (immediately right of Q) = seat 4. T (immediately left of P) = seat 1. R takes the only remaining seat, 5 (the rightmost end, consistent with the clue). Order: T, P, Q, S, R.

prompt: Six colleagues (A, B, C, D, E, F) sit in a row of six chairs, left to right. C sits at the leftmost end. D sits immediately to the right of A. B sits immediately to the right of D. F sits immediately to the right of B. E sits immediately to the right of F. Where does A sit?
explanation: C occupies seat 1. The chain A-D-B-F-E forms a block of 5 consecutive people, and only seats 2-6 remain, so this block must fill them in order: A=2, D=3, B=4, F=5, E=6. A sits second from the left.

prompt: Six people sit evenly spaced around a circular table, facing outward, away from the table: J, K, L, M, N, O. K sits second to the right of J. L sits immediately to the left of K. M sits directly opposite J. N sits immediately to the right of M. Where does O sit?
options: Immediately to the left of M
Immediately to the right of K
Immediately to the left of J
explanation: Numbering seats 1-6 clockwise with J at 1: K (second to the right) is at 3, L (immediately left of K) is at 2, M (opposite J) is at 4, N (immediately right of M) is at 5. The only remaining seat is 6, which is immediately to the left (counterclockwise neighbor) of J, so O sits there.

prompt: Six colleagues sit around a circular table facing outward, away from the table: R, S, T, U, V, W. T sits immediately to the right of R. U sits second to the left of T. V sits directly opposite U. S sits immediately to the right of V. Where does W sit relative to R?
options: Second to the left of R
Immediately to the right of R
Immediately to the left of R
explanation: Numbering seats 1-6 clockwise with R at 1: T=2, U (second to the left of T) = 6, V (opposite U) = 3, S (immediately right of V) = 4. The only remaining seat is 5, for W. Going counterclockwise from R (1→6→5), W is two seats to the left of R.

prompt: In a race, five runners (Ana, Cara, Ben, Dan, and Emma) finish in distinct positions with no ties. Ana finishes before Ben but after Cara. Ben finishes before Emma. Dan finishes last. Who finishes first?
explanation: The clues establish the chain Cara before Ana before Ben before Emma, and Dan is explicitly last. Combining these: Cara, Ana, Ben, Emma, Dan, so Cara finishes first.

prompt: Five students scored differently on a test: Mia, Noah, Olivia, Paul, and Quinn. Noah scored higher than Paul but lower than Mia. Olivia scored the highest of all. Quinn scored lower than Paul. Who scored the lowest?
explanation: Take the clues one at a time. "Noah higher than Paul but lower than Mia" gives Mia above Noah above Paul. "Quinn lower than Paul" extends the chain to Mia, Noah, Paul, Quinn. "Olivia highest of all" puts Olivia above Mia, so the full order from highest to lowest is Olivia, Mia, Noah, Paul, Quinn. Quinn is at the bottom. Paul is the tempting answer because he is named as scoring lower than Noah, but the last clue places Quinn below him, and Mia is second rather than last because only Olivia outscores her.

prompt: Six chess players (A, B, C, D, E, F) are ranked 1st (best) through 6th (worst), with no ties. C ranks immediately below A. E ranks exactly three places below B. D ranks 2nd. F ranks better than C but worse than B. What is A's rank?
explanation: Testing each possible rank for A (with $C = A+1$) against the remaining constraints, only A = 5th works: this forces C = 6th, and among the remaining ranks {1, 3, 4} for B, E, F, only B = 1st, E = 4th (three below B), F = 3rd satisfies both "E is three below B" and "$B < F < C$" ($1 < 3 < 6$). All other values for A lead to a contradiction with at least one clue.

prompt: A seven-story building has floors numbered 1 (bottom) to 7 (top), each occupied by a different family: J, K, L, M, N, O, and P. L lives on floor 4. M lives immediately below L. N lives on the topmost floor. K lives three floors above J. O lives immediately above K. Which floor does J live on?
explanation: L=4 and M=3 (immediately below L). N=7 (topmost). The remaining floors {1, 2, 5, 6} must hold J, $K = J+3$, $O = K+1$, and P. Testing J=2 gives K=5 and O=6, all within the remaining set with P=1 left over: the only value of J that works without conflict. J lives on floor 2.

prompt: A six-story building has floors numbered 1 (bottom) to 6 (top), each occupied by a different resident: A, B, C, D, E, F. D lives on floor 1. C lives directly above D. E lives on floor 3. F lives directly below B. B lives on an even-numbered floor. Which floor does A live on?
explanation: D=1, C=2 (directly above D), E=3. Remaining floors {4, 5, 6} go to A, B, F with $F = B-1$ and B even. Testing B=4 gives F=3, which conflicts with E; so B=6, F=5, leaving A=4 as the only remaining floor.

prompt: Five boxes (P, Q, R, S, T) are stacked one on top of another. Q is at the very bottom. R is at the very top. R is directly above T. S is directly below P. Which box is directly above Q?
explanation: Numbering positions 1 (bottom) to 5 (top): Q=1, R=5, T=4 (directly below R). The remaining positions {2, 3} go to S and P with S directly below P, so S=2 and P=3 (the only valid pairing). The box directly above Q (position 1) is S at position 2.

prompt: Four boxes (A, B, C, D) are placed in a stack. Box A is at the bottom. Box B is directly on top of Box D. Box C is directly on top of Box B. What is the order from bottom to top?
explanation: A occupies the bottom position. The chain D-B-C (B above D, C above B) forms a consecutive block of 3, which must fill the remaining three positions in order: D, then B, then C. Order from bottom to top: A, D, B, C.

prompt: Eight students are divided into two teams of four for a project: Team X and Team Y. Priya is on Team X. Liam is on Team Y. Noah is on the same team as Liam. Sam is on a different team from Priya. Which team is Sam on?
explanation: There are only two teams, so "a different team from Priya" leaves exactly one possibility. Priya is on Team X, therefore Sam is on Team Y. "Cannot be determined" is tempting because the clues about Liam and Noah are never needed and their presence suggests more work is required, but a two-way split means ruling out one team settles the other. "Both teams" is impossible, since the eight students are divided into two teams of four and each student occupies one seat in that split.

prompt: Six friends (J, K, L, M, N, O) sit in a row of six chairs, numbered 1 to 6 from left to right. L sits third from the left. N sits second from the right. J sits immediately to the left of L. Exactly one person sits between L and O. M sits immediately to the right of N. Who sits at seat 1?
explanation: L=3 and N=5 (second from the right of 6). J=2 (immediately left of L). "Exactly one person between L and O" means O is at position 1 or 5, but 5 is taken by N, so O=1. M=6 (immediately right of N), leaving K=4. Seat 1 is occupied by O.

prompt: Five people (A, B, C, D, E) sit evenly spaced around a circular table, all facing outward, away from the table. B sits second to the right of A. C sits immediately to the left of B. D sits immediately to the right of B. Where does E sit relative to A?
options: Second to the left of A
Immediately to the left of A
Immediately to the right of A
Second to the right of A
explanation: Numbering seats 1-5 clockwise with A at 1: B (second to the right) = 3, C (immediately left of B) = 2, D (immediately right of B) = 4. The only remaining seat is 5, for E, which is the counterclockwise neighbor of A, i.e., immediately to the left of A.

prompt: Five people (Amy, Ben, Cleo, Dev, and Ella) stand in a line for a photo, numbered position 1 to 5 from left to right. Amy is at position 1. Ben is not at either end. Cleo is somewhere to the right of Ben. Dev is immediately to the left of Ella. Ella is not at position 5. Cleo is not adjacent to Ella. What is Ella's position?
explanation: Amy=1. Dev and Ella must be consecutive (Ella immediately after Dev) within positions {2,3,4,5}, and Ella is not at position 5, leaving two candidate pairs: (Dev=2,Ella=3) or (Dev=3,Ella=4). Testing (Dev=3,Ella=4) forces Ben=2 and Cleo=5, but then Cleo is adjacent to Ella, violating the "not adjacent" clue. So (Dev=2,Ella=3) is the only valid case, with Ben=4 and Cleo=5. Ella sits at position 3.

prompt: Four friends (W, X, Y, Z) sit evenly spaced around a square table, facing outward, away from the table. X sits directly opposite W. Y sits immediately to the right of W. Where does Z sit relative to X?
options: Immediately to the left of X
Immediately to the right of Y
Immediately to the right of X
explanation: Numbering seats 1-4 clockwise with W at 1: X (opposite W) = 3, Y (immediately right of W) = 2. The only remaining seat is 4, for Z, which is the clockwise neighbor of X (seat 3), i.e., immediately to the right of X.

prompt: Seven students sit in a row of seven chairs, numbered 1 to 7 left to right. G sits at seat 1. D sits immediately to the right of G. F sits three seats to the right of D. B sits immediately to the left of F. The remaining students, A, C, and E, occupy the remaining seats, with C sitting immediately to the right of E. Which seat does A occupy?
explanation: G=1, D=2, F=5 (three seats right of D), B=4 (immediately left of F). The remaining seats {3, 6, 7} go to A, C, E, with C directly right of E. The only consecutive pair within {3, 6, 7} is (6, 7), so E=6, C=7, leaving A=3 by elimination.

prompt: In a certain code, each letter is replaced by the letter 2 positions before it in the alphabet, so "GARDEN" is written as "EYPBCL". How is "FLOWER" written in the same code?
explanation: Shifting each letter of FLOWER back by 2: F→D, L→J, O→M, W→U, E→C, R→P, giving "DJMUCP".

prompt: In a code language, "sun rises east" is written as "pit dor kaf", "sun sets west" is written as "pit lom naz", and "moon rises west" is written as "ruv dor naz". What is the code for "rises"?
explanation: Comparing sentences 1 and 3, both contain "rises" and both codes share the word "dor": no other word or code is common to both, so "rises" = "dor". (Cross-checking: "sun"="pit" from sentences 1-2, "west"="naz" from sentences 2-3, leaving "east"="kaf", "sets"="lom", "moon"="ruv" with no conflicts.)

prompt: Eight students are divided into two teams of four for a project: Team X and Team Y. M and N are on different teams. O is on the same team as M. P is on the same team as N. M is on Team X. Exactly two of Q, R, and S are on Team X. Q is on Team X. R is on the same team as Q. T is on a different team from M. Which team is T on?
explanation: M=X, so O=X (same as M) and N=Y (different from M), so P=Y (same as N). Q=X and R=X (same as Q), and since exactly two of Q, R, S are on Team X, S must be Y. Team X now has M, O, Q, R (four), so Team Y must hold N, P, S, and T, four each. T is on Team Y, which also follows directly since T is stated to be on a different team from M (Team X).

prompt: In a code, each letter is replaced by the letter immediately after it in the alphabet, and then the whole word is reversed. Using this rule, "CAT" becomes "UBD" (C→D, A→B, T→U gives DBU, then reversed gives UBD). Using the same rule, what does "LION" become?
explanation: Shift each letter forward by one: L→M, I→J, O→P, N→O, giving "MJPO". Reversing this string gives "OPJM".

prompt: Seven colleagues (A, B, C, D, E, F, G) sit in a row of seven chairs, numbered 1 to 7 from left to right. B sits two seats to the right of A. C sits immediately to the left of B. D sits at seat 7. E sits exactly two seats to the right of F. G does not sit at seat 1. A sits to the left of F. Where does A sit?
explanation: D=7. With $B = A+2$, $C = B-1$, and $E = F+2$, testing A=1 gives B=3, C=2; the remaining seats {4,5,6} then need F and E with $E = F+2$, which only F=4,E=6 satisfies, leaving G=5 (not seat 1, consistent with the clue, and A=1 is indeed left of F=4). No other value of A satisfies every constraint at once. A sits at seat 1.

prompt: Pointing to a man, Riya says, "He is the son of my father's sister." How is the man related to Riya?
explanation: Riya's father's sister is Riya's aunt. The aunt's son is Riya's cousin.

prompt: A is a man. Pointing to B, A says, "B's mother is my mother's only daughter." How is A related to B?
explanation: Since A is male, he cannot be his own mother's "only daughter", so that daughter must be A's sister, who is B's mother. A is therefore the brother of B's mother, making A the boy's/girl's uncle.

prompt: Sam is a woman. Pointing to a photograph, Sam says, "The girl's father is the only son of my mother." How is the girl related to Sam?
explanation: Since Sam is female, she cannot be her own mother's "only son", so that son must be Sam's brother, who is the girl's father. Sam is therefore the girl's father's sister, i.e., the girl's aunt.

prompt: P is the brother of Q. Q is the daughter of R. R is the husband of S. S has only one daughter, Q. T is the son of S. How is T related to P?
explanation: Q is the daughter of R and S. P, being Q's brother, is also a child of R and S. T, being a son of S (and thus of the couple R and S), is likewise their child. Since P and T are both children of the same parents, T is P's brother.

prompt: Arjun says, "I have as many brothers as sisters." His sister Meena says, "I have twice as many brothers as sisters." How many sons and daughters do their parents have?
explanation: Let $b$ be the number of sons and $g$ the number of daughters. Arjun (a son) has $b-1$ brothers and $g$ sisters; "equal" gives $b - 1 = g$. Meena (a daughter) has $b$ brothers and $g-1$ sisters; "twice as many" gives $b = 2(g-1)$. Substituting $b = g+1$ into the second equation: $g + 1 = 2g - 2$, so $g = 3$ and $b = 4$. The family has 4 sons and 3 daughters.

prompt: Find the next number in the series: 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, ?
explanation: Each term follows the pattern $a_{n+1} = 2a_n + 1$. $63 \times 2 + 1 = 127$.

prompt: Find the next letter in the series: A, C, F, J, O, ?
explanation: The gaps between letter positions increase by one each time: A(1)→C(3) is +2, C→F(6) is +3, F→J(10) is +4, J→O(15) is +5. The next gap is +6, giving position 21, which is U.

prompt: Find the missing term in the series: 2A, 4C, 8E, 16G, ?
explanation: The numbers double each time (2, 4, 8, 16, 32), and the letters skip forward by two positions each time (A, C, E, G, I). The next term is "32I".

prompt: Find the next number in the series: 1, 4, 9, 18, 35, ?
explanation: The differences between consecutive terms are 3, 5, 9, 17, and the differences of those differences double each time (2, 4, 8, next 16). So the next difference is $17 + 16 = 33$, giving the next term as $35 + 33 = 68$.

prompt: Eight people (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H) sit evenly spaced around a circular table, all facing outward, away from the table. B sits directly opposite A. C sits two seats clockwise from B. D sits immediately to the left of C. E sits immediately to the right of A. F sits two seats clockwise from E. G sits immediately to the right of C. Where does H sit relative to A?
options: Second to the right of A
Second to the left of A
Third to the right of A
explanation: Numbering seats 1-8 clockwise with A=1: B (opposite A) = 5. C (two seats clockwise from B) = 7. D (immediately left of C) = 6. E (immediately right of A) = 2. F (two seats clockwise from E) = 4. G (immediately right of C) = 8. The only remaining seat is 3, for H, which is two seats clockwise from A, i.e., second to the right of A.

prompt: A man walks 6 km east, then turns left and walks 6 km, then turns left again and walks 6 km. How far and in which direction is he from his starting point?
explanation: East 6 km, then left turn (north) 6 km, then left turn again (west) 6 km. The east and west legs cancel out (6 km each, opposite directions), leaving only the 6 km northward displacement from the middle leg.

prompt: Point B is 8 km north of Point A. Point C is 6 km east of Point B. Point D is 8 km south of Point C. What is the direction and distance of Point D from Point A?
explanation: Using coordinates with A at $(0,0)$: $B = (0,8)$, $C = (6,8)$, $D = (6,0)$. The north ($+8$) and south ($-8$) legs cancel, leaving D directly 6 km east of A.

prompt: Facing north, Riya turns 90° clockwise and walks 4 km, then turns 90° clockwise again and walks 3 km. What is the shortest distance between her starting point and her current position?
explanation: Turning 90° clockwise from north faces her east; walking 4 km east gives $(4,0)$. Turning 90° clockwise again faces her south; walking 3 km south gives $(4,-3)$. The straight-line distance is $\sqrt{4^2+3^2} = 5$ km.

prompt: A cyclist starts at point O, rides 10 km north to point P, then 6 km west to point Q, then 10 km south to point R, then 2 km east to point S. What is the shortest distance from S to O, and in which direction is O from S?
explanation: Using coordinates with O at $(0,0)$: $P = (0,10)$, $Q = (-6,10)$, $R = (-6,0)$, $S = (-4,0)$. The north and south legs (10 km each) cancel, leaving S 4 km west of O; equivalently, O is 4 km east of S.

prompt: In a class of 50 students, 6 students play neither football nor cricket. The number of students who play only cricket is exactly twice the number who play only football. 14 students play both football and cricket. How many students play only football?
explanation: Students playing at least one sport = $50 - 6 = 44$. Let $x$ = students playing only football, so only cricket = $2x$ (given). Then $x + 2x + 14 = 44$, so $3x = 30$, giving $x = 10$ students who play only football.

prompt: A seven-story building has floors numbered 1 (bottom) to 7 (top), each occupied by a different tenant: A, B, C, D, E, F, G. B lives exactly three floors above A. C lives exactly two floors below B. D lives on floor 1. E is exactly one floor above F. G does not live on the top floor. A lives above floor 1 but below floor 4. Which floor does A live on?
explanation: D=1. Testing A=2 (satisfying "above floor 1, below floor 4"): $B = A+3 = 5$, $C = B-2 = 3$. The remaining floors {4,6,7} then need E and F consecutive with $E = F+1$, which only F=6,E=7 satisfies, leaving G=4 (not the top floor, consistent with the clue). Testing A=3 instead forces B=6, C=4, leaving {2,5,7} for E,F,G with no consecutive pair available for E=F+1, so that case fails. A lives on floor 2.

prompt: In a group of 200 people, 90 read Newspaper A, 80 read Newspaper B, 70 read Newspaper C, 30 read both A and B, 25 read both B and C, 20 read both A and C, and 10 read all three. How many people read none of the three newspapers?
explanation: By inclusion-exclusion: $|A \cup B \cup C| = 90 + 80 + 70 - 30 - 25 - 20 + 10 = 175$. People reading none = $200 - 175 = 25$.

prompt: If January 1, 2023 was a Sunday, what day of the week was January 1, 2024? (2023 has 365 days, since it is not a leap year.)
explanation: 365 days is exactly 52 weeks plus 1 extra day ($365 = 52 \times 7 + 1$), so the day of the week advances by one: Sunday + 1 = Monday.

prompt: Six students (A, B, C, D, E, F) scored differently on a test, ranked 1st (highest) through 6th (lowest), with no ties. B ranked immediately below A. D ranked exactly two places below C. E ranked 6th. F did not rank 1st. A ranked better than C. Who ranked 1st?
explanation: E=6th. With $B = A+1$ and $D = C+2$, and A better (lower-numbered) than C, testing A=1 gives B=2; the remaining ranks {3,4,5} then need C and D exactly two apart, which only C=3,D=5 satisfies, leaving F=4 (not 1st, consistent with the clue). No other value of A satisfies every constraint at once. A ranked 1st.

prompt: At what time between 3 and 4 o'clock will the minute hand and hour hand of a clock be exactly opposite each other (180° apart)?
explanation: At $t$ minutes past 3:00, the hour hand is at $90 + 0.5t$ degrees and the minute hand is at $6t$ degrees. Setting the minute hand 180° ahead: $6t - (90 + 0.5t) = 180$, so $5.5t = 270$, giving $t = \frac{270}{5.5} = 49\frac{1}{11}$ minutes.
